INTRODUCTION TO
ECONOMICS

Two Tech Cities, One Tough Choice
Once there were two neighbouring technology cities, Techville and Innovia. Both 
received ₹500 crore, 500 engineers, limited land, electricity, and water to build a 
world-class technology industry.
Techville decided to use most of its resources to produce semiconductors. At first, 
production increased rapidly and everyone celebrated. But soon the city faced 
electricity shortages, water scarcity, pollution, and a shortage of engineers in other 
sectors.
Innovia made a different choice. It divided its resources between semiconductors, 
AI, healthcare, and infrastructure. It also encouraged factories to save electricity and 
water. Its chip production was lower than Techville's, but its overall productivity 
and quality of life were higher.
One day, a Techville engineer asked: “Why didn't we simply use all our resources to 
produce more chips?” The economist smiled and replied: “Because resources are 
limited. Every choice has a cost. When you choose one use, you give up another.”
If you had ₹500 crore, 500 engineers, and limited resources, what would you
produce and what would you be willing to give up?

India’s Renewable Energy Market — 2019–2025
India’s renewable energy sector has undergone significant changes in recent years 
because of developments in technology, government policy, electricity 
consumption, production costs, infrastructure, and global energy markets. In 2019, 
India continued expanding solar and wind power as electricity consumption 
increased and renewable-energy projects received greater policy support. In 2020, 
the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted construction activities, transportation, equipment 
deliveries, and supply chains for renewable-energy projects. In 2021, global 
shortages of solar modules and other essential components, together with 
disruptions in international supply chains, created challenges for renewable-energy 
project developers. In 2022, international energy-market disruptions increased 
attention toward energy security and alternative energy sources, while India 
continued promoting renewable-energy investment and capacity expansion. In 2023, 
the rapid adoption of solar power, technological improvements, and increasing 
investment in renewable-energy infrastructure contributed to strong growth in the 
sector, while electricity consumption also increased because of economic activity 
and growing use of electrical equipment and digital technologies. In 2024, India 
continued adding substantial renewable-energy capacity, particularly through solar 
power, supported by policy initiatives, technological developments, and private 
investment; at the same time, constraints related to transmission networks, land, 
equipment availability, and grid integration remained important. In 2025, the 
renewable-energy sector continued to expand, with increasing attention not only to 
solar and wind generation but also to battery storage, green hydrogen, smart grids, 
and other technologies needed to manage the changing electricity system.

The Smartphone Chip Market
In Bengaluru, Arjun, the manager of a semiconductor company, watched his 
factory produce thousands of computer chips used in smartphones, laptops, and 
electric vehicles. One year, production was excellent, and the company produced a 
large quantity of chips. Confident about strong demand, Arjun set the price at 
₹1,000 per chip. But Priya, the procurement manager of a smartphone company, 
shook her head at the high price. “I cannot afford to buy chips at this price. Our 
production cost will become too high,” she complained. Soon, other electronics 
manufacturers also reduced their orders, and Arjun was left with a large stock of 
unsold chips. The very next year, a shortage of raw materials and strong demand for 
smartphones and EVs reduced chip production significantly. Arjun initially offered 
the chips at ₹600 per chip, and manufacturers rushed to buy as many as they could. 
Soon, the available chips were insufficient to meet demand, and manufacturers 
began competing for the limited supply. Seeing the situation, Mr. Rao, a 
policymaker, explained, “We need a market price where the quantity of chips 
supplied equals the quantity demanded.” Finally, when the price settled at ₹800 per 
chip, Arjun could sell his chips, Priya could obtain the required components, and 
manufacturers could continue producing smartphones and EVs

Coca-Cola and World War II
During World War II, the Coca-Cola Company set 
up over 60 bottling plants in Europe and the Pacific 
to serve American soldiers. More than 5 billion 
bottles were delivered between 1943 and 1945. As 
soldiers introduced locals to the drink, demand 
increased in areas where Coca-Cola had never been 
sold before. However, the production capacity 
remained fixed due to wartime resource constraints. 
The increased popularity created long lines and high 
local demand, but supply couldn’t immediately 
increase.

The 1972 U.S.–Soviet Grain Deal
In 1972, the Soviet Union quietly bought around 10 
million tons of wheat and corn from the U.S. due to 
a poor harvest. These deals were made without

unexpected fall in U.S. stockpiles. As a result, the 
price of wheat jumped from $1.73 to over $4.89 per 
bushel in just a few months. This sudden export led 
to shortages and price spikes in other countries, 
especially those that depended on U.S. grain 
imports. Supply increases: P ↓ Q↑

During 2007–2008, the corn market went through a

Controls on Prices
A legal maximum on the price at 
which a good can be sold.
Price Ceiling
Price Floor
A legal minimum on the price 
at which a good can be sold.

The American Association of Ice-Cream Eaters complains that 
the $3 price is too high for everyone to enjoy a cone a day (their 
recommended daily allowance).
Meanwhile, the National Organization of Ice-Cream Makers 
complains that the $3 price—the result of “cutthroat 
competition”—is too low and is depressing the incomes of its 
members.
Each of these groups lobbies the government to pass laws that 
alter the market outcome by directly controlling the price of an 
ice- cream cone.
When the government, moved by the complaints and campaign 
contributions of the Ice-Cream Eaters, imposes a price ceiling 
on the market for ice cream, two outcomes are possible. 
A. The government imposes a price ceiling of $4 per cone.
B. The government imposes a price ceiling of $2 per cone.

Price ceiling
In the 1940s, as World War II created a housing crunch, New York 
City introduced rent control laws to keep housing affordable for 
returning soldiers and low-income families. The rent ceiling meant 
that landlords could not raise rents, even as demand for apartments 
surged. In the short run, this provided temporary relief. However, 
over the decades, the policy led to long-term shortages of rental 
housing. Landlords, receiving below-market rents, often neglect 
maintenance, leading to deteriorating buildings. At the same time, 
new construction slowed down, as developers were discouraged by 
the low profit potential. By the 1970s and 1980s, it was clear that 
the policy, though well-intentioned, had led to severe mismatches 
in housing demand and supply, just like a binding price ceiling. 
The result was long waiting lists, informal payments ("key 
money"), and discrimination in apartment allocation, as landlords 
informally selected tenants they preferred.

Imagine now that the government is persuaded by 
the pleas of the National Organization of 
Ice-Cream Makers whose members feel the $3 
equilibrium price is too low. In this case, the 
government might institute a price floor. 
When the government imposes a price floor on 
the ice-cream market, two outcomes are possible. 
A. The government imposes a price floor of $2 
per cone when the equilibrium price is $3.
B. Th government imposes a price floor of $4 per 
cone.

Price floor
In the United States during the 1930s, the government 
introduced the first federal minimum wage through the Fair 
Labor Standards Act of 1938. At that time, the law mandated a 
minimum wage of $0.25 per hour, aimed at improving the living 
standards of low-income workers during the Great Depression. 
While the intention was to ensure a basic level of income, the 
policy had unintended effects in certain sectors. In regions 
where the market wage was naturally below the new legal 
minimum, employers found it too expensive to retain the same 
number of workers. As a result, youth and unskilled workers 
faced layoffs or reduced working hours. This mimicked the 
effect of a binding price floor: when the wage (price of labor) 
was set above the equilibrium, the quantity of labor supplied 
(workers willing to work) exceeded the quantity demanded (jobs 
offered)—creating unemployment in the affected segments. 
Over time, adjustments in skills, productivity, and inflation 
reduced these frictions, but the early years showed clear signs of 
surplus labor, particularly among minority and low-skilled youth 
populations.

CONSUMER 
SURPLUS

The extra benefit that consumers receive when they are willing to pay 
more for a good or service than the actual market price they pay.
In other words: Willingness to pay – Actual price paid.

The Jio Launch and Consumer Surplus in the Indian Telecom Market
In September 2016, Reliance Jio Infocomm Limited (Jio) disrupted the Indian 
telecom market by launching free voice calls and extremely low-cost 4G data plans. 
Before Jio's entry, leading telecom players such as Airtel, Vodafone, and Idea were 
charging around ₹250–₹300 per GB of mobile data.
Jio offered 4G data at ₹50 per GB or less, and for the first few months, it offered 
completely free voice and data services. This radically changed consumer behavior 
and created massive consumer surplus across the country.

agricultural departments and farmers’ cooperatives, varied between

facilities, and input use.

Market Efficiency
A market is said to be efficient when resources are allocated in the best possible 
way, so that total welfare (consumer surplus + producer surplus) is maximized.

Indian Railways — A Monopoly in Public Transport
Indian Railways (IR) is one of the largest railway networks in the world and operates under the Government of 
India. It runs trains across the country and carries millions of passengers and tons of goods every day. Because 
only one company — Indian Railways — provides railway services across India, it is considered a monopoly. In 
this market, there are no close substitutes for railways because other transport options like buses or flights cannot 
carry as many people or goods at such a low cost.
Indian Railways sets its own prices with government approval, which means it is a price maker. It charges very 
low fares for passengers to make travel affordable for everyone. However, it charges higher rates for freight 
(goods transport) to cover its costs. This method of using profits from one group (freight) to support another 
(passengers) is called cross-subsidization. It helps poor passengers travel at a low price, but it also causes losses 
because the fares are often below the actual cost of running trains.
The government keeps control of Indian Railways because building a separate railway network is very expensive 
and requires large investments in land, tracks, and trains. If many companies tried to build their own networks, it 
would lead to duplication and waste of resources. That is why Indian Railways is called a natural monopoly — 
one company can serve the whole country more efficiently than several competing firms.
Although Indian Railways helps the public by providing cheap and reliable transport, it faces some problems. 
Trains are often crowded, delayed, and underfunded because the low fares reduce the profit needed for 
maintenance and upgrades. To improve efficiency, the government has started allowing private trains on some 
routes and has also promoted digital ticketing through IRCTC.

Game theory is a mathematical tool that helps to study strategic situations in which players 
optimize a variable not only based on their own preferences but also on other players’ 
decisions and reactions
Widely used in pricing, advertising, negotiation, and market entry.

Types of Games
2 Person-Zero sum game: A game with two players, where one player's gain equals the other's 
loss, is known as a two-person zero-sum game. The sum of their net winning is zero. It is also 
a rectangular game because the payoff matrix is rectangular.

A strategy is a predetermined rule that specifies completely how one intends to respond to 
each possible circumstance at each stage of the game.
1. Pure Strategy: If the player selects the same strategy each time. In this case, each 
player knows what other players would do against his selected strategy.
2. Mixed Strategy: When the players use a combination of strategies and each player leaves 
the other player guessing as to what he would do, in case the other adopts a certain 
strategy.

The Nash Equilibrium is the point in a game where no player can improve their own

Minimax-Maximin Principle 
The selection of an optimal strategy by each player without the knowledge 
of the competitor’s strategy is the basic problem of playing games. The 
objective of the study is to know how these players select their respective 
strategies so that they may optimize their payoff. Such a decision-making 
criterion is referred to as the minimax-maximin principle.
Saddle Point
If the minimax value = maximin value, then the game is said to have a 
saddle (equilibrium) point.

Procedure to determine Saddle (Equilibrium) Point
• Select the minimum element in each row of the payoff matrix and write them under the “row 
minima” heading. Then select the largest element among these elements and enclose it in a 
rectangle.
• Select the maximum element in each column of the pay matrix and write them under the 
“column maxima” heading. Then select the lowest element among these elements and 
enclose it in a circle.
• Find out elements that are the same in the circle as well as the rectangle and mark the 
position of such elements on the matrix. This element represents the value of the game and is 
called a saddle point.
